discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: A strong frontal system will impact Western Washington today with widespread rain, gusty winds, and coastal flooding. Precipitation chances will linger into Friday with a weaker system. A brief break in precipitation is expected this weekend as a weak ridge builds over the Pacific Northwest. An active weather pattern resumes early next week.
hydrology: A frontal system will bring an additional 1 to 3 inches of rainfall to the region today with snow levels as high as 6000-7000 feet. The bulk of the moisture is expected over the Olympic Peninsula and along the coast. While area rivers will likely experience rises, no widespread river flooding is expected.

The exception is the Skokomish River, where a River Flood Warning remains in effect through Friday. The Skokomish will remain in moderate flood stage into this afternoon. The Skokomish is expected to fall below flood stage on Friday, with additional rises possible into next week.

The incoming heavy rainfall through Thursday may also pose a hazard to the Bear Gulch burn scar, which has been sensitive to precipitation so far this winter season. A handful of small landslides have already occurred on the burn scar, and additional landslides in this area cannot be ruled out this week as heavy rain continues over the Olympic Peninsula.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A strong frontal system will impact Western Washington today with widespread rain, gusty winds, and coastal flooding. Precipitation chances will linger into Friday with a weaker system. A brief break in precipitation is expected this weekend as a weak ridge builds over the Pacific Northwest. An active weather pattern resumes early next week.

sections.title: Short term (today through Saturday)
paragraphs: A strong warm front reached the central Washington coast around midnight as evidenced by a quick veer to strong southerly wind and a spike in temperature at Hoquiam. Windy conditions will continue through the morning and spread to Puget Sound as the warm front lifts northward across the interior. A trailing cold front will push inland this afternoon for a transition to a post-frontal unstable air mass with showers and isolated thunderstorms. Winds will ease behind the front.

A much weaker system riding over the northern periphery of a ridge to our south will spread some light rain back across the area by Friday afternoon, but QPF and wind will be much less of a factor with this system. A low amplitude upper ridge will shift onshore across the Pacific Northwest on Saturday for a brief drying trend and a return to seasonal temperatures.

Coastal flooding will continue to be a concern today as astronomical high tides combine with storm surge and high surf to produce some significant tidal anomalies and impacts to coastal communities. Coastal flooding impacts are expected to peak for the inland waters today before tides gradually weaken.

sections.title: Long term (Saturday night through Wednesday)
paragraphs: A weak upper ridge axis is expected to shift east of the area Saturday night. Another upper trough is expected to move into the offshore waters on Sunday, but ensembles lack any significant cohesion with its evolution. It's worth noting that the 00Z operational run of the GFS spins up another sub 980 millibar surface low offshore by Sunday night. Given the potential impacts to holiday travel, we'll have to keep an eye on this.

Moving forward into the first half of next week, model disagreements persist. There is some hint of another short-lived dry break in the Wednesday timeframe. Current forecasts for the period have near normal temps and a generic chance of rain. In other words, a near climo forecast for early December.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Breezy and wet conditions early this morning with a mixed bag of conditions across western Washington. As a front moves through the area this morning, heavier batches of rain have put most terminals in MVFR/IFR conditions, with some interior terminals seeing VFR as well. Additionally, heavier rain has brought reductions in visibilities, generally around 2-5 SM. Expect this trend throughout most of the morning. Precipitation will become more showery in nature later this afternoon, which will allow ceilings to improve to MVFR/VFR across the area. There is a 15-25% chance of thunderstorms across most of the area this morning into the afternoon hours, with confidence being low in occurrence to put in the TAF at this time.

S/SE gusty winds this morning, with gusts up to 25 to 35 kts for interior locations. Strongest winds continue to be along the coast for HQM and near BLI, where gusts up to 40 to 45 kts continue to be possible this morning. Winds will remain elevated throughout the afternoon, with a notable decrease this evening, with southwesterly winds gusting up briefly up to 15 kts by 00z.

KSEA...VFR conditions this morning in rain and breezy winds. Heavier rain moving through the terminal this morning could drop conditions down to MVFR at times, along with reductions in visibilities 3 to 5 SM. Rain will transition into more showery in nature, allowing for more broken ceilings and a return to more VFR conditions over the terminal. Additionally, there remains a 15% chance of thunderstorms this afternoon, however confidence continues to remain low.

Breezy S/SE this morning with sustained winds 15 to 20 kts, with potential gusts up to 30 kts. Winds will remain breezy through the afternoon with a notable decrease by 00z, turning southwesterly and sustained 10 to 15 kts, with gusts up to 15 to 20 kts.
Mazurkiewicz

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A strong frontal system will continue to cross over the waters this morning, bringing strong winds and elevated seas to area waters. A Gale Warning remains in effect for all coastal water zones, and all interior zones; the exception being the East Entrance of the Strait of Juan De Fuca, where a Storm Warning continues. A Small Craft remains in the Central Strait of Juan De Fuca. Thunderstorms are also favored to develop over the coastal waters early this morning and move inland towards the inner waters throughout the day, producing localized lightning, gusty winds, and small hail.

Winds will start to decrease this evening over the waters, with a Small Craft Advisory out for the coastal waters, mainly for continued elevated wind and seas. Conditions will start to calm heading into Friday, with a weak system approaching the waters, however impacts should remain minimal. High pressure is favored to develop over the waters through the weekend, with seas and winds to ease, the exception is the Strait of Juan De Fuca, where a westerly push of winds is likely.

Seas around 15 to 20 feet this morning will hover in this range throughout the majority of the day, slowly decreasing this evening into Friday morning around 10 to 15 feet. Seas will lower even further by late Friday into Saturday, where we could see seas get below 10 feet through the weekend. Seas are favored to rise above 10 feet into next week.
Mazurkiewicz

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Wet and windy conditions expected for Thanksgiving Day as an atmospheric river traverses the region. Coastal flooding and active marine conditions also continue as high winds and rough seas coincide with monthly King Tides. Another system will bring additional rain on Friday before dry weather and offshore winds return this weekend. Active weather likely to return early next week with more rain and wind.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Wet and windy conditions expected for Thanksgiving Day as an atmospheric river traverses the region. Coastal flooding and active marine conditions also continue as high winds and rough seas coincide with monthly King Tides. Another system will bring additional rain on Friday before dry weather and offshore winds return this weekend. Active weather likely to return early next week with more rain and wind.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Wednesday...Thanksgiving Day opens with an ongoing atmospheric river as a broad swath of poleward moisture transport precedes a cold front which is moving inland over the Olympic Peninsula as of early this morning. Rain is already underway over much of the region and is expected to continue into the afternoon. The heaviest rainfall rates are likely to be located near or just ahead of the surface cold front, which will steadily move to the southeast today. Peak rainfall rates of 0.2-0.4 inches per hour are most likely to occur (20-50% chance at any time) before 6 AM to the north and west of Portland, between 4-8 AM in the Portland/Vancouver metro, central Willamette Valley, and central Oregon coast, and between 6-10 AM in the southern Willamette Valley and at the Cascade Passes. These rainfall rates could result in nuisance flooding of urban, low-lying, or other poor drainage areas, and Flood Advisories may be needed through midday. Drivers should plan to encounter wet roads, localized standing water, and limited roadway visibility during heavy rain. More widespread flooding or river flooding is not anticipated as the duration of heavy rain will be too short to produce problematic rainfall accumulations. Winter driving conditions are very unlikely at the Cascade Passes as snow levels remain above 6-8 kft.

The cold frontal passage will also produce a period of gusty south winds, particularly along the immediate coast and in higher elevations of coastal terrain. A High Wind Warning remains in effect along the entire coast north of Lane County through 7 AM this morning. The majority of gusts will peak at 50-60 mph, but some gusts over 60 mph should be expected, most likely at exposed headlands or ridgetops or possibly on bridges near the coast. Away from the coast, the highest winds are expected in higher elevations of the Coast Range and Willapa Hills where a Wind Advisory remains in effect through 10 AM. Peak gusts in these areas are more likely to be near 50 mph. Winds will weaken behind the frontal passage, but breezy conditions with gusts to around 40 mph are likely to linger into the afternoon. Some downed trees or power lines and resultant isolated to scattered power outages should be expected today. Elsewhere inland, peak wind gusts of 40-45 mph this morning may yield isolated impacts, with breezy conditions lingering through the afternoon.

Behind the departing cold front, a drier period can be expected this afternoon through tonight with scattered post-frontal rain showers persisting across the region. A trailing area of surface low pressure will move into the region on Friday, bringing another round of rain. While not corresponding to canonical AR dynamics, this feature will nonetheless be able to tap into the same moisture stream with more westerly mid-level flow oriented perpendicular to area terrain features promoting a stronger orographic enhancement of rainfall. That is all to say that despite the weaker synoptic support, this second system may be just as capable of producing periods of heavy rainfall rates, bringing continued chances for nuisance urban or poor-drainage flooding on Friday. Consensus is higher that peak vapor transport will be located over west-central Oregon, meaning areas south of Portland will be most likely to see the heaviest rainfall rates of 0.2-0.4 inches per hour from the late morning through the mid-afternoon. There continues to be uncertainty in the intensity of this surface low at it moves onshore on Friday, with low chances (10-15%) for peak wind gusts over 50 mph along the Lincoln and Lane County coasts, corresponding to ensemble members with the deepest surface lows. Chances for peak gusts above 45 mph inland are 5% or less. More likely, gusts will peak around 30-40 mph on the central coast, and 20-30 mph inland south of Salem.

Brief and transient upper-level ridging passes overhead on Saturday, favoring drier weather with offshore flow to begin the weekend. East winds are expected to peak Saturday night into Sunday morning in the Cascades and typical east-west oriented terrain gaps including the Columbia River Gorge. A pressure gradient peaking at -4 to -5 mb between Portland and the Dalles, which should support peak gusts in the Gorge of 40-50 mph, and 20-30 mph in the eastern Portland/Vancouver metro. There is good consensus that wet weather returns Sunday into Monday, although the details of the synoptic pattern remain uncertain at this lead time. Snow levels are expected to trend downward, perhaps below 5 kft by Monday, which may allow for snow at the Cascade Passes, but that aspect of the forecast is also low confidence. Drier conditions may return midweek as the progressive pattern of recent weeks continues overhead. -36

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12z Friday...A strong cold front is traversing the airspace early this morning, extending from the central OR coast near KTMK to the northeast into the central WA Cascades as of 12z Thu and tracking to the southeast through the next 6-12 hours. Where the heaviest rain is occurring, terminal observations show vis/cigs restricted MVFR inland and IFR along the coast. This pattern is likely to continue as the front progresses, with MVFR conditions favored at Portland-area and Willamette Valley terminals from roughly 14-17z Thu as rainfall rates peak. Behind the boundary, sct low clouds and light rain showers may linger while cigs rebound to VFR (60-70% chance) by 14-16z Thu along the coast and by 17-18z Thu inland. The southern Willamette Valley may be an exception where MVFR cigs are more persistent. Cigs trend back down to MVFR elsewhere after 03-06z Fri as low stratus develops overnight.

Gusty winds are also expected during the frontal passage. Peak gusts in excess of 45-50 kt are most likely along the coast through 14-16z Thu, while inland terminals instead peak at 25-35 kt between 14-17z Thu. These winds are largely out of the S to SW, however Portland-area terminals will instead see SE flow ahead of the boundary. Strong winds of 50-70 kt out of the SSW at 2 kft above the surface will support low-level speed shear across the region as the front passes, but the addition of directional shear at Portland-area terminals merits LLWS groups in the TAF until winds veer out of the south after 14-15z Thu. Winds then tend to ease across the airspace through the remainder of the period.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR conditions with gusty SE winds will continue ahead of the approaching cold front, with strong low- level wind shear as SSW winds at 2 kft above the surface reach 50-60 kt. The frontal passage from 14-17z Thu will see cigs likely (80% chance) lowering to MVFR, while periods of restricted vis should also be expected during the heaviest rainfall rates. Winds will veer out of the south during the frontal passage, with shear weakening as winds aloft fall behind the boundary. Cigs likely (70% chance) lift back to VFR after 17z Thu, with lingering rain showers and S winds of 10-15 kt. Winds further ease to around 5 kt this evening while chances for MVFR cigs increase as low stratus develops overnight. -36

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A strong frontal system is traversing the waters early this morning, bringing continued hazardous marine conditions. Widespread gales are ongoing, with localized storm- force winds most likely within 10 NM between Cape Shoalwater and, very appropriately, Cape Foulweather, where winds are accelerated within a coastal jet. Winds will ease behind the frontal boundary, with Storm and Gale Warnings expected to expire at 7 AM this morning. A persistent southwesterly swell near 15 ft at 13 seconds with very steep wind-driven seas are yielding combined seas near 20 ft early this morning, which will also ease behind the boundary. Hazardous Seas Warnings remain in effect across the waters from 7 AM today through 1 AM Friday as seas steadily ease to below 15 ft. Small Craft Advisories will then be in effect from 1 AM Friday through 1 AM Saturday until seas fall below 10 ft. There continues to be 20-35% chances that another area of surface low pressure moving onshore over the central Oregon coast on Friday will be strong enough to produce another round of gales south of Cape Lookout.

A brief break in the active weather will see calmer marine conditions on Saturday, although the progressive pattern is very likely to bring additional weather systems into the region early next week. -36

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: The combination of King Tides and elevated seas leading to tidal overflow continue to support a Coastal Flood Advisory through today for the north and central Oregon coast, and through Friday for the south Washington coast. Impacts during this period are most likely in the hours around high tide. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water, and take appropriate action to protect life and property. There is also a continued moderate to high sneaker wave threat through Friday. Beachgoers should exercise caution, stay far back from incoming waves, and remain observant of the ocean. Avoid logs, large rocks, and jetties.

summary.headline: High surf and strong atmospheric river for Oregon coast
summary.lede: Today into tomorrow, a strong atmospheric river impacts Northwest Oregon with high surf along the coast. Snow levels fall well below pass level in the Cascades and Whistler BC, with a marginal risk of thunderstorms on the Washington coast today.
